text:
Aryabhata was India's first satellite, named after a fifth-century Indian astronomer. It went up on a Soviet rocket. Five years later, India reached orbit on a rocket of its own.

In July 1975, at the height of the Cold War, an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz met in orbit. Commanders Thomas Stafford and Alexei Leonov shook hands through the open hatch. It was the last flight of an Apollo spacecraft.

Viking 1 was the first spacecraft to land on Mars and keep working. Its orbiter mapped the planet, while the lander sent the first pictures from the surface and tested the soil for life, with results that are still argued over. The lander kept working for more than six years.

Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn. Then, in 1990, it turned around and photographed the Earth as a pale blue dot, from six billion kilometers away. In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space. It is the farthest object we have ever made, and it is still sending data home.

Navstar 1 was the first G P S satellite. Each one carries atomic clocks and broadcasts the time, and a receiver that can hear four of them can work out where it is. The full set of twenty-four was ready in 1995. Today, billions of phones listen to them.

On Christmas Eve, 1979, Europe launched a rocket of its own. Ariane 1 was built so that Europe would not need anyone else to launch its satellites, and it was the first rocket designed mainly for commercial customers. Its successors still fly from French Guiana.

On April twelfth, 1981, twenty years to the day after Gagarin, Columbia launched like a rocket and came home like a glider: the first reusable spaceship. Five orbiters flew a hundred and thirty-five missions. Two of them, Challenger and Columbia, were lost, with fourteen crew.

T D R S One was the first of NASA's relay satellites. From high above the equator, they let spacecraft in low orbit talk to the ground almost all the time, not only when passing over a station. Its booster went out of control, and controllers spent nearly three months nudging it into place with its small thrusters. It worked for twenty-six years.

Mir was the first space station assembled in orbit from separate modules, added one by one over ten years. Valeri Polyakov stayed aboard for four hundred and thirty-seven days in a row, still the record for a single flight. After fifteen years, Mir was brought down into the Pacific.

In November 1988, the Soviet space shuttle Boo-rahn made its first and only flight, with no one on board. Its computers flew two orbits and landed it on a runway at Baikonur, even choosing an extra turn on the way in because of gusty winds. The program was cancelled, and in 2002, Boo-rahn was destroyed when the roof of its hangar collapsed.

Magellan was the first planetary probe launched from the Space Shuttle. Partly built from spare parts of other missions, it looked through the thick clouds of Venus with radar, and mapped almost the whole planet: volcanoes, lava plains, and surprisingly few craters.

Galileo was the first spacecraft to orbit an outer planet. Its big antenna never opened, so it sent everything home through a small one. In December 1995, its probe dived into Jupiter's clouds. At the end, Galileo itself was flown into Jupiter, so it could never contaminate the moon Europa.

In April 1990, the shuttle Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope above the blur of the atmosphere. Its main mirror turned out to be ground very slightly wrong, and astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993. Shuttle crews serviced it five times. Thirty-six years later, it is still observing.

Ulysses studied the Sun from above its poles. No rocket could tip its orbit that far, so it flew out to Jupiter first, and used Jupiter's gravity to swing up, out of the plane of the planets. It passed over the Sun's poles three times.

The Compton Gamma Ray Observatory was one of the heaviest science satellites ever flown. Over nine years, it recorded thousands of gamma-ray bursts, and found that they come evenly from every direction, the first strong clue that they happen far beyond our galaxy.

Soho has watched the Sun for three decades, from a point one and a half million kilometers toward it, and many space-weather warnings come from it. Amateurs searching its pictures have found more than five thousand comets, more than any other telescope.

Cassini spent thirteen years at Saturn. Its European probe, Hoygens, landed on the moon Titan, the farthest landing ever made. Cassini found geysers of water on Enceladus, and seas of methane on Titan. Low on fuel, it was flown into Saturn in 2017, so it could never contaminate those moons.

In November 1998, a Russian rocket launched Zarya, the first piece of the International Space Station. Built by the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada, the station has had people aboard every day since November 2000, longer than any other spacecraft.

Stardust flew through the dust around comet Vilt 2, and caught grains of it in a collector the size of a tennis racket. Its capsule came home in 2006 at twelve point nine kilometers a second, the fastest reentry of any human-made object. In the dust, scientists found glycine, an amino acid.

The Chandra X-ray Observatory sees the X-rays given off by black holes, exploding stars and clusters of galaxies. It was the heaviest payload the Shuttle ever launched, on the first Shuttle flight commanded by a woman, Eileen Collins. Its long orbit takes it a third of the way to the Moon.

Opportunity was built to last three months on Mars. It kept exploring for more than fourteen years, found rocks that formed in water, and drove more than a marathon. In 2018, a planet-wide dust storm covered its solar panels, and it never woke up.

Spitzer, the last of NASA's four Great Observatories, saw the universe in infrared: the heat glow of dust, newborn stars and distant galaxies. It was the first spacecraft to trail the Earth around the Sun, away from Earth's heat. When its coolant ran out, it kept working, warm, for another ten years.

In October 2003, Yang Lee-way made China the third country to send a person into orbit on its own rocket. His Shen-joe spacecraft looks like a Soyuz, only larger. Today, China runs a space station of its own.

After ten years and four planetary flybys, Rosetta caught up with a comet and flew alongside it for two years. Its lander, Fee-lay, made the first landing on a comet, bouncing twice before it came to rest in a shadow. At the end of the mission, Rosetta was set down on the comet too.

Messenger was the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury. Getting there took six planetary flybys and six and a half years, to shed enough speed. It confirmed that there is water ice in shadowed craters at Mercury's north pole. Out of fuel, it was crashed into the planet in 2015.

January 2007. China tests an anti-satellite missile on one of its own retired weather satellites, Fung-yoon one C, more than eight hundred kilometers up. The impact makes the largest debris cloud ever recorded: more than three and a half thousand pieces big enough to track. At that height there is almost no air to slow them down. Nearly twenty years later, more than two thousand three hundred are still up there.

Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two worlds beyond the Earth: the giant asteroid Vesta, and the dwarf planet Ceres. Its ion engines were so gentle that at full power they took four days to reach a hundred kilometers an hour. But they never stopped. Out of fuel, Dawn still circles Ceres.

In September 2008, on its fourth try, SpaceX's Falcon 1 became the first privately developed liquid-fuel rocket to reach orbit. It launched from a tiny island in the Pacific, carrying a dummy satellite. The first three launches had failed. Falcon 1 flew only once more, and made way for Falcon 9.

February 2009. For the first time, two whole satellites collide by accident. A working Iridium phone satellite and a dead Russian military satellite meet almost at right angles, at nearly twelve kilometers a second. Nobody was steering Kosmos twenty-two fifty-one, and the close pass had not been flagged. Since then, operators are warned of close approaches, and move their satellites out of the way.

Kepler stared at one patch of sky for four years, watching a hundred and fifty thousand stars for the tiny dip in light when a planet passes in front. It confirmed more than twenty-six hundred planets, and showed that most stars have them, and that many are about the size of Earth.

Falcon 9 first flew in June 2010. Since December 2015, its first stage has flown back and landed upright, so the same booster can launch again and again. One booster has flown thirty-six times, and Falcon 9 has launched more than six hundred and seventy times.
